newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Sudan argues against sanctions, defends human rights.
newsitem.headline: Sudan argues against sanctions, defends human rights.

text.p: Sudan's foreign minister sought to ward off a threatened United Nations air embargo and said attacks against his country's human rights record were often linked to criticism of Islam in general.

Speaking to the U.N. General Assembly on Monday, Ali Osman Mohammad Taha said "persistent attempts to impose sanctions on Sudan defies logic and justice and needs to be reconsidered in order to alleviate the injustice inflicted on my country."

The Security Council on August 16 imposed an air embargo on Sudan but delayed putting it into effect for at least three months depending on a U.N. report on whether Khartoum was complying with the council's demands.

The sanctions, which already include diplomatic and travel embargoes, target Sudan for its failure to extradite three Egyptians accused of taking part in a plot to kill President Hosni Mubarak shortly after he arrived in Addis Ababa on June 26, 1995 for a summit of the Organisation of African Unity.

Taha said there was no concrete evidence of Khartoum's involvement in harbouring the suspects. Ethiopia, he said, had conducted a secret trial and condemned to death the three men it had captured after the Mubarak assassination attempt.

He also said his government had conducted fair elections and signed a political charter between two factions of rebels in the Christian and animist south rebelling against the Khartoum. He said that Sharia (Islamic) law still left open the possibility of "complimentary legislation" in each state that would guarantee religious freedom.

Sudan has been accused by human rights groups of supressing dissent and political parties, condoning slavery, forcing Islamic law on non-believers, discriminating against women and periodically preventing international relief aid from reaching starving civilians in enemy territory.

Appealing for cultural diversity, Taha said that criticism of Sudan was often linked to images of Islam as barbaric and prone to terrorism. "These malicious allegations are unjust and Islam is completely innocent from such allegations."

"Islam is the religion of tolerance and coexistence. Therefore, we call upon the international community to stop this ferocious campaign targeting Islam and call upon the United Nations to distance itself from such campaigns," he said.
